exercise.title: Why is approximation without a remainder only a hope?

statement.p: A Taylor polynomial gives a computable piece of a function. The remainder is the part not yet captured. In your own words, why is the approximation looks reasonable not yet a mathematical statement, and what question does the remainder force you to answer?

hint.p: Looking nearby is not a bound. The remainder asks how large the gap can be, which is the only way an approximation gets a scale.

paragraphs.title: A local warning
paragraphs.p: But at x=2, the same partial sums are

The problem is not the function. The function is defined at x=2. The problem is that the power series centered at 0 has radius 1. A Taylor polynomial is built from local information. It should not be trusted far from its center without an error estimate.

exercise.title: What controls the size of a Taylor error?

statement.p: The Lagrange remainder bound involves a bound M on the next derivative, the distance |x-a|^{n+1}, and a factorial (n+1)!. In your own words, why do those three ingredients explain both why Taylor polynomials are local and why higher degree can still help?

hint.p: Far from the center, the power of distance grows. Close to the center, that power is small, and dividing by a factorial makes higher-degree leftovers even smaller if the next derivative is not too wild.

exercise.title: Why is Taylor’s theorem a higher-order Mean Value Theorem?

statement.p: After subtracting a Taylor polynomial, the function and the polynomial agree through many derivatives at the center. In your own words, why do those many zeros invite Rolle’s Theorem, and why does a higher derivative then appear in the remainder?

hint.p: Many zeros at one point, together with one extra zero of the error at x, produce an intermediate point where a higher derivative vanishes or is forced to a definite value. That is the Mean Value Theorem in a higher-order costume.

paragraphs.title: Why the formula is true
paragraphs.p: A more useful repeated version is this: each integration by parts pulls out one Taylor term at a, and leaves an integral involving one higher derivative.
Repeating the same step gives the general formula.
This form is optional for computation, but important for the story. Taylor’s theorem is not magic. The error is an accumulated effect of higher derivatives.

exercise.title: Why are there two useful languages for Taylor error?

statement.p: The Lagrange form bounds the next derivative. The integral form writes the remainder as accumulated next-derivative information. Alternating estimates apply when Taylor terms bounce and shrink. In your own words, why do these views complement one another rather than compete?

hint.p: One form is built for a worst-case bound. One form shows the remainder as an accumulation, the same idea as the Fundamental Theorem. Alternation is a special mechanism that names the next omitted term as the gap.
